summary: A fleet can now be upgraded a few appliances at a time instead of all at once. Plan a rollout to a specific version and the control plane divides the estate into RINGS — a canary first — asks each ring to install that exact version over the existing control channel, and refuses to start the next ring until the current one has proved itself. Proving itself means three things, not one: every node in the ring came back on the control channel, REPORTED the target version itself, and held that state for a settle window. Those catch three different ways an upgrade goes wrong — a node that never returns, a node that returns still running the old build because the swap silently failed, and a node that boots, looks perfectly healthy, and falls over a minute later. The control plane can judge any of this because it now records what each appliance says it is running, captured from the control-channel greeting that already carried it. Nodes that cannot replace their own binary at all — a container image, a package-managed install — are identified while the rollout is being PLANNED, listed with the way they are actually upgraded instead, and left out of the rings rather than discovered by a canary that fails on one. The rollout screen for all of this is the API and the audit trail; every plan, start, halt and completion is recorded.
compatibility: Purely additive: two new tables through the normal auto-migrator, two new read-only fields on the node record, and new endpoints on each side (GET /api/system/update/apply now accepts an optional pinned version on a node; GET/POST /api/fleet-rollouts* on the control plane, readable by any fleet role and writable only by a superadmin). Nothing changes for an operator who upgrades appliances by hand. TWO BEHAVIOUR CHANGES ON THE NODE, both deliberate. Its updater now looks a release up BY TAG rather than asking GitHub for whatever is newest — required, because a canary ring is meaningless if the node resolves 'latest' for itself, and it also means the updater no longer depends on this repository's three other products continuing to publish their releases as non-latest. And it now REFUSES A DOWNGRADE, with an explanation, before anything is overwritten: swapping a binary back is easy but the database it then opens is not reversible, because migrations here are forward-only, so an older build can meet a schema it has never seen. FOR THE SAME REASON THERE IS NO AUTOMATIC ROLLBACK. A ring that fails stops the rollout, leaves every appliance that has not been touched on the version it was already running, and waits for a person; a fleet is recovered by rolling FORWARD to a fixed build, which this same machinery does. Live-benched against a real two-node fleet on the real fleet CA and control channel. That bench found a real gap on its first run: the rollout was planning across nodes that could never self-update and only learning so when the canary halted, which is now detected while planning. 21 mutations of the health gate and the node's guards were all caught by the tests.
